text.p: The U.S. Treasury market faces a void of fresh economic news on Wednesday, leaving it nothing to concentrate on but Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's recapitulation of his Senate Humphrey Hawkins testimony -- this time to the House of Representatives.

The market expects Greenspan to express the same sentiments in his House appearance that he offered the Senate last week. Variations on his main themes could come in the question and answer period, analysts said, but the tone of his remarks will remain consistent.
The hawkish tone of Greenspan's speech last week has soured market sentiment and has sent bond prices to new lows in nearly every session since.

"Greenspan has two choices," said William Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "He could either echo what he said last week or he could clarify or soften his message. What people believe is that he will send a message that is consistent with what he said last week. He's said the Fed is vigilant, that it is forward-looking, and that if necessary, it will fire a pre-emptive shot to ward off inflation pressures.
"That's what the market expects him to say and it has positioned itself pretty well for that," said Hornbarger.
William Sullivan, senior vice president and fixed-income research director at Dean Witter Reynolds, also said Greenspan would not change the tone of his testimony on Wednesday.

Sullivan noted that in an appearance before the House Budget Committee on Tuesday, Greenspan said his intent is to explain the thinking and considerations of Federal Reserve policy makers, not to move markets.
"That might lessen the chance of any adverse reaction to his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday," said Sullivan.

"Not that he's backing away from his remarks, but he's reminding market participants that he doesn't have a specific value in mind for equities or for the Treasury bond yield," Sullivan said. "He's just saying that among the many things policymakers must determine is whether these financial market developments would contribute to imbalances in economic activity that could imply upward pressure on living costs."
Sullivan said the market has already reacted to Greenspan's views and bond prices reflect them.

While the power of Greenspan's remarks to move prices might be limited on Wednesday, the market has taken on a distinctly bearish flavor in the last week that it might not soon escape, said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial market economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.

"It was supposed to be an easy three days between the NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Management) report on Monday and the (February) payroll employment report on Friday," said Rupkey. "We were supposed to see more and more short-covering. But for some reason we've barrelled on down here -- touching 6-7/8 percent (on the 30-year bond yield)."

Rupkey said the market looks weak. Referring to the dollar's close in New York on Tuesday at a 34-month high against the mark, Rupkey said, "If you can't get the bond market going up with dollar mark above 1.70, a key psychological level, you can bet foreigners aren't buying and supporting the bond market like they used to."

But Sullivan said dollar strength might give the bond market some help on Wednesday. "The dollar strength is clearly a friendly development," he said. "In a data vacuum, maybe we can focus on that a bit more."
Federal funds are likely to open between 5-3/16 percent and 5-1/4 percent, dealers indicated.
